[PAPER_0058, relevance_score=0.339] Our Study

In the present study, we aimed to replicate the date/delay effect in intertemporal choice (Read et al., 2005) and examine its attentional mechanisms using eye tracking. Our preregistered hypotheses were as follows.

Generally, we hypothesized that we would observe lower discount rates, that is, less discounting of larger-later rewards, in the date compared to the delay condition (Hypothesis 1).

[PAPER_0059, relevance_score=0.313] Moreover, based on the candidate explanations of the date/delay effect in the literature, we made a number of predictions about (oculomotor) behavior: First, if participants indeed adopt a more deliberative processing mode due to the higher cognitive demands in the date compared to the delay condition (i.e., dates are more complex than delay units), this should be observable in reaction times (RTs) as well as in the number of saccades and fixations (Horstmann et al., 2009).

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.373] Particularly, we expected that in the date condition, participants would show higher RTs and, consequently, a higher total number of saccades and fixations compared to the delay condition (Hypothesis 2a).

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.394] As the attention-focusing hypothesis (Read et al., 2005) and the hypothesis of stronger deliberation (Dshemuchadse et al., 2013) imply potentially different predictions (attentional hypothesis: longer fixation durations on reward attributes because rewards are more highly weighted; deliberation hypothesis: longer fixation durations on time attributes because of the need to adapt to dates), we formulated an undirected hypothesis: We hypothesized that attentional focus would shift toward either reward attributes or time attributes in the date condition (as compared to the delay condition), as represented by longer mean cumulative fixation durations either on reward or time attributes (Hypothesis 2c).

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.369] Longer fixation durations on reward (vs. time) attributes in the date compared to the delay condition would be in favor of the attention-focusing hypothesis, while longer fixation durations on time (vs. reward) attributes would be in favor of the hypothesis of stronger deliberation.

Finally, we hypothesized that eye movement data (saccades and/or fixation durations) would be associated with interindividual differences in the magnitude of the date/delay effect (Hypothesis 3).

[PAPER_0131, relevance_score=0.332] Descriptive statistics indicated that nearly all participants showed the date/delay effect in the expected direction ( Supplement B in the online supplemental materials ).

Nonpreregistered, explorative within-subject t tests of subjective ratings of cognitive demand, frustration, fatigue, and worry did not reveal any significant differences between conditions (Table 1).

[PAPER_0190, relevance_score=0.313] Scholten & Read, 2010), participants appeared to place a higher weight on reward than time values in the date compared to the delay condition. While the results generally support the attention-focusing hypothesis (Read et al., 2005), the name of the hypothesis might be somewhat misleading since it does not seem to be necessary to direct overt visual attention more strongly toward rewards in the date compared to the delay condition. Rather, the weighting of the reward attributes relative to the time attributes appears to be increased (LeBoeuf, 2006), resulting in a reward-weighting hypothesis.

items.deviation_information:
The principal hypotheses broadly correspond. However, the registered expectation of higher date-condition mental demand was to be explicitly tested, whereas the paper calls that test nonpreregistered and exploratory [PREREG_0055] [PAPER_0131]. The registered directional pupil-dilation and predecision saccade-vigor predictions were not found in the provided paper excerpts, despite coverage of attentional hypotheses [PREREG_0056] [PREREG_0057] [PREREG_0058] [PAPER_0059] [PAPER_0066]. The paper also advances a reward-weighting hypothesis that need not involve increased overt reward attention; this formulation was not found in the provided registration excerpts [PAPER_0190] [PAPER_0201] [PREREG_0010]. The positive directional prediction for comparative-search change and the condition-specific response-time predictions were not found explicitly stated in the paper excerpts, although related correlations were examined [PREREG_0045] [PREREG_0054] [PAPER_0066] [PAPER_0157]. The paper refers to supplementary material, which is not part of the input; missing elements may be reported there.

items.deviation_information:
The paper accepted at least 20 usable eye-tracking trials per condition rather than usable data for every choice, and explicitly discloses this change. [PREREG_0047] [PAPER_0069] [PAPER_0214] Mandatory responses for all questions and a general rule excluding participants for essential data missing because of technical errors were not found in the provided paper excerpts; the paper refers to supplementary material, which is not part of the input. [PREREG_0049] [PAPER_0077] [PAPER_0006] The paper reports one participant without an indicated educational classification, but the excerpts do not establish why or whether this constituted an incomplete questionnaire. [PAPER_0072]
